messages.subject_clean: impact of the scale of observations in poisson regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I don't quite understand why the scale of the observations in a poisson model affect so much the results.

I can demonstrate what I mean borrowing from the example in the documentation for the poisson likelihood, I simulate data from a latent predictor and a scaled offset. I get completely different results depending on the scale of the measurements.

I must be missing something really silly, but I'm confused right now. Thanks for any insight.

ƒacu.-

inla_poisson <- function(scale = 1) {
  set.seed(123)
  n=100
  a = 1
  b = 1
  z = rnorm(n)
  eta = a + b*z
  E = scale * sample(1:10, n, replace=TRUE)
  lambda = E*exp(eta)
  y = rpois(n, lambda = lambda)
  data = list(y=y,z=z)
  formula = y ~ 1+z
  result = inla(formula, family = "poisson", data = data, E=E)
  summary(result)
}

messages.body_plain:
When the data is fixed and only E is changed, then the intercept is all that should change. However, in the test code here the simulated data matches the rescaled E, so neither mean estimate should be expected to change much (except due to possible issues with lack of information, as in the lambda < 1 case, as you mention).

In the first case, the uncertainty should be essentially unchanged (the intercept is on the log-scale, and E just introduces a deterministic shift).
In the second case, the posterior variance should be smaller for large lambda.

That means that the change in variances seems reasonable, but not the change in the intercept estimate, since the test code does case 2, not case 1.

So I ran the code myself.
The  lambda  average is 25.7 for scale=1 and 25700 for scale=1000.
...and I’ll switch to my laptop for the rest of the results.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: INLA for distributional regression (predictors on parameters of distributions)
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

I am trying to fit distributional regression models with INLA (regression models similar to gamlss, i.e., generalized additive models on the parameters of a distribution rather on its mean), but I cannot find appropriate resources on the help page.

I've come across the paper (below) which states in page 1073 that distributional regression is not supported by INLA. Is this still true (if it was)? If not, how could I fit a model, for example gaussian model, with one gam on the mean and another on the standard deviation and get their corresponding fitted values, please? The vignette for gaussian models includes an example for mu only (not tau). The question is not restricted to gaussian models and could be equally valid for any distribution with more than 1 parameter.

Example

y_i ~ F(mu_i, tau_i, xi_i), where F depends upon covariates x1, ..., x6, through
mu_i = f1(x1) + f2(x2) + ...,
tau_i = f3(x3) + f4(x4) + ...,
xi_i = f5(x5) + f6(x6) + ...

I would expect something like

formula = y~f(x1, model="rw2") + f(x2, model="rw2"), how to include those for tau and xi?
fit <- inla(formula, data=data, control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE))
mu <- fit$summary.fitted.values[...]
tau <- fit$summary.fitted.values[...]
...

Thanks for your help!

 <http://goog_54856652>
Klein, N., Kneib, T. et al. (2016). Scale-Dependent Priors for Variance Parameters in Struc- tured Additive Distributional Regression. Bayesian Analysis 11  <http://goog_54856658>1071–1106.  <http://1071–1106.>https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdfview_1/euclid.ba/1448323525

Hi,

The inlabru package is intended to be able to handle some such models. A parametric distribution model is part of the tutorials linked on inlabru.org <http://inlabru.org> (spatially dependent animal group size distribution), but nonparametric versions is just a matter of including such components in the model definition, like you describe. The main idea is that inlabru allows the user to specify fairly general R expressions, which allows the model components to enter in places where inla cannot have them. What we’ve done so far involves point process formulations of the problem. We’re working on generalizing and working out properties of the method, so we haven’t published the specifics on distribution estimation with this approach yet.

Finn

messages.subject: Spatially varying logistic regression with large data - INLA is crashing
messages.subject_clean: Spatially varying logistic regression with large data - INLA is crashing
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA enthusiasts,

I am struggling with the implementation of a spatially varying logistic regression for very large data.

The research question:

 I want to explore which population group in which locations is most at risk for a specific disease. As I have information on individual level, I want to use logistic regression. However, I need to account for regional differences as I have very large urban areas and sparsely populated rural areas, so you may expect that e.g. migration background and availability of healthcare are more important in urban areas than in rural areas. That`s why the model of choice ultimately is a spatially varying logistic regression.

The data:

The dataset consists of 1.6 million anonymized persons distributed across 1,600 municipalities. For each person I have individual information (e.g. age, gender, employment status, migration background, previous diseases and so on) and several variables at the municipality level (e.g. one-person-households, availability of healthcare). The outcome variable - the disease in question is a binary variable coded as 1 - has the disease - 0 does not have the disease. The variables gender, employment status and migration background are also coded as binary variables (0/1). Age, number of previous disease and percentage of one-person-households are continuous variables. I ensured that the data is formatted how INLA needs it (e.g. area ids of the data match with the ids of the graph file).

The approach:

First I created a non-spatial logistic regression, which does its job as expected. Then I proceeded to the Bayesian SVC model using the following formula:

model_svc <- inla(DISEASE~   1  +
                    f(idx1, female, constr = TRUE, model = "besag",
                      graph = "graph_v3") +
                    f(idx2, nr_of_previous_diseases, constr = TRUE, model = "besag",
                      graph = "graph_v3") +
                    f(idx3, unemployed, constr = TRUE, model = "besag",
                      graph = "graph_v3") +
                    f(idx4, migration_background, constr = TRUE, model = "besag",
                      graph = "graph_v3") +
                    f(idx5, one_person_households, constr = TRUE, model = "besag",
                      graph = "graph_v3") +
                    f(idx6, GPs_available, constr = TRUE, model = "besag",
                      graph = "graph_v3") +
                  f(idx7, age, constr = TRUE, model = "besag",
                    graph = "graph_v3"),
                  family = "binomial", data=data, control.compute = list(dic=T),
                  control.inla = list(diagonal = 1000, strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb"))

If I run the model with a small subset of 20.000 persons, it works, but if I run the model with a larger sample of 50.000 persons, INLA crashes. Ultimately, I need to run the analysis with all 1.6 million persons. Based on some suggestions, I included "control.inla = list(diagonal = 1000, strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb"). This however, alters only the processing time when run for a small sample but INLA still crashes for a larger sample, regardless whether I use the diagonal argument or not. I will admit that I don`t know yet how to calculate starting values or determine reasonable precision parameters if that plays a role for this problem. I have a server with 32CPU and 256 GB memory, so my available hardware is not the issue. Unfortunately, I cannot provide sample data as restrictions apply.

What should I do to make the model run for all 1.6 million persons?

Any help in this regard is greatly appreciated.

Best, Boris

messages.body_plain:
I've run big analyses like this, and had crashes. The simple, if
unhelpful, answer is to get more memory. Another solution might be to
ignore the spatial effect and fit the random slopes as iid (or even as
fixed effects, as interactions with region). If this works, it should
help you simplify the model by showing you which effects do not vary
spatially, and hopefully that will remove a few spatial effects from
the final model.

Bob

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Mean of the random field
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Mean of the random field
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the reason the mean of a random field is often assumed to be zero is
just that it simplifies model construction in additive models.
Since we can change the mean of a model by adding something new, we
can also change random field to have zero mean by subtracting
whatever the mean is, and moving that mean to a new model component.
A common traditional viewpoint in spatial statistics is to
construct the model in stages, so that linear covariate effects define
the (conditional) mean of a random field:

mean = X beta
field|mean ~ N(mean, dependence)
eta := mean
obs|field ~ p(.|eta)

When building models where random fields have zero mean we instead
write the above model as

mean = X beta
field ~ N(0, dependence)
eta := mean + field
obs|field ~ p(.|eta)

The resulting estimates of "mean" and "eta" are unchanged by this
reformulation, which is a simple reparameterisation of the model.
This means that for many models we don't need to be able to specify a
non-zero mean, since we can just put that in other parts of the model.

For more general hierarchical models it can sometimes be convenient to
have some explicit non-zero mean model directly in the random field
specification, but one can always extract the mean part into its own
component if components are allowed to be deterministic.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Boris,

So I don't' think I can help you on the technical side of making this model run, but, something does strike me about the model specification on the setting of the data description you gave.

You said that you have individual level data (e.g. gender) and municipality level data (e.g. one person households). Yet in your model you are modelling both gender and one person households as a besag model with graph_v3 as the neighbourhood graph. To me this begs the questions: 1) How are you generating this graph_v3?, and 2) why are you applying the same graph geometry to individual level data, and municipality level data? In my experience (admittedly limited), the besag model is applied at the municipality level, since it represents the spatially structured effects by areas, so I don't understand why you are applying it to gender. Also, to specify gender as a spatially structured variable in the first place implies that you believe the effect of gender on disease risk varies by location. Do you have a good a-priori reason to believe this? Because without a disease specific prior belief for this, I would find this unusual. Similar comment for age and number of previous diseases - is their a good reason to believe there are spatially structured effects from such variables?

I have a suspicion here that what you actually want to do is model "fixed effects" for the individual level variables and spatially structured effects for the municipal level variables. In which case your model would look simpler - something like:

model_svc <- inla(DISEASE ~ 1 +  female + age + unemployed + migration_background + nr_of_previous_diseases_Er +

  f(idx5, p_one-person-households, constr = TRUE, model = "besag",
    graph = "graph_v3", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.01)))) +

  f(idx7, GPs_available, constr = TRUE, model = "besag",
    graph = "graph_v3", scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.01)))),
  f(idx8, model = "iid", hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.01)))),
family = "binomial", data=daten1, control.compute = list(dic=T),
control.inla = list(diagonal = 10000, strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb"), verbose = TRUE)

Perhaps such a model will be easier to fit on 1.6million people ? (note I am assuming graph_v3 depicts the neighborhood graph of the municipalities)

James

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Mean of the random field
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Mean of the random field
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

thank you for your replies. I understand that you can substract a known mean from the model to get a zero-mean field, but what approach do i choose when the mean is not known? Maybe you can refer me to a tutorial or paper where "mean = X beta" is explained (i.e. how to choose beta)?

> For more general hierarchical models it can sometimes be convenient to
> have some explicit non-zero mean model directly in the random field
> specification

How would that "non-zero mean model directly in the random field" look like?

@help help

> so the mean here is
>         \mu + \beta x(s)

How do i specify  and ?

Regards,
Tim

Am Montag, 6. August 2018 15:42:39 UTC+2 schrieb Finn Lindgren:

> Hi,
>
> the reason the mean of a random field is often assumed to be zero is
> just that it simplifies model construction in additive models.
> Since we can change the mean of a model by adding something new, we
> can also change random field to have zero mean by subtracting
> whatever the mean is, and moving that mean to a new model component.
> A common traditional viewpoint in spatial statistics is to
> construct the model in stages, so that linear covariate effects define
> the (conditional) mean of a random field:
>
> mean = X beta
> field|mean ~ N(mean, dependence)
> eta := mean
> obs|field ~ p(.|eta)
>
> When building models where random fields have zero mean we instead
> write the above model as
>
> mean = X beta
> field ~ N(0, dependence)
> eta := mean + field
> obs|field ~ p(.|eta)
>
> The resulting estimates of "mean" and "eta" are unchanged by this
> reformulation, which is a simple reparameterisation of the model.
> This means that for many models we don't need to be able to specify a
> non-zero mean, since we can just put that in other parts of the model.
>
> For more general hierarchical models it can sometimes be convenient to
> have some explicit non-zero mean model directly in the random field
> specification, but one can always extract the mean part into its own
> component if components are allowed to be deterministic.
>
>
> Finn
>
> On 6 August 2018 at 14:13, Tim H. <tim.hei...@onlinehome.de> wrote:
> > Hello,
> >
> > are there any statistical models for the mean of a random field? Often the
> > mean is assumed to be zero. So what model can i choose if the mean is not
> > zero but dependent on the location. Are there functions (similar like the
> > Matern function for the covariance) for the mean of a field?

On 8 August 2018 at 09:18, Tim H. <tim.hei...@onlinehome.de> wrote:

> Hello,
>

> thank you for your replies. I understand that you can substract a known mean from the model to get a zero-mean field, but what approach do i choose when the mean is not known? Maybe you can refer me to a tutorial or paper where "mean = X beta" is explained (i.e. how to choose beta)?

The "X beta" part is just shorthand for "some linear fixed effect effects part your model" but could be replaced by anything (e.g. other random effects).

> > For more general hierarchical models it can sometimes be convenient to
> > have some explicit non-zero mean model directly in the random field
> > specification
>
> How would that "non-zero mean model directly in the random field" look like?

That was referring to general modelling principles, not INLA package syntax.

> @help help
> > so the mean here is
> >         \mu + \beta x(s)
>
> How do i specify  and ?

Exacly as in the example given,

response ~ 1 + x + f(...)

1 gives an intercept, the \mu above.
x gives a linear effect of the covariate, with slope \beta (called x in the summary output).
f(...) gives a zero mean random field.

It's not that one needs to _know_ the unknown mean of the radon field; we simply move the unknown parts outside of the definition of the random field.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Precision
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Precision
messages.body_plain:
Precision = 1 / Variance

if you rather want the posterior for the stddev, you can do as follows.
for other models you have to chose the correct hyperparameters. the
'internal' gives the posterior in the internal scale, which is
log(precision), so the change of variable becomes stdev =
sqrt(1/exp(log.precision))

> r = inla(y~1,data = data.frame(y=1:10))
> names(r$internal.marginals.hyperpar)
[1] "Log precision for the Gaussian observations"
> m.sd <http://m.sd> = inla.tmarginal(function(x) sqrt(1/exp(x)),
r$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]])
> inla.zmarginal(m.sd <http://m.sd>)
Mean            2.94156
Stdev           0.690075
Quantile  0.025 1.94294
Quantile  0.25  2.4522
Quantile  0.5   2.82296
Quantile  0.75  3.2955
Quantile  0.975 4.63018
> plot(inla.smarginal(m.sd <http://m.sd>), type="l", xlab = "stdev", ylab =
"posterior(stdev)")

Many thanks in advance.

Boris

messages.subject: lognormal regression and estimates interpretation
messages.subject_clean: lognormal regression and estimates interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Good evening,

I have a question about the correct interpretation of the estimates provided by R-INLA when running a LogNormal regression. This is probably trivial for everyone on this forum but I am looking for the exact proper wording to go with it and how it would differ from running a normal regression of log-transform response.

Here is a slight extension of example code form this website, with an additional fixed effect:

require(INLA)
n = 300
x1 = c(scale(runif(n)))
x2 = c(scale(runif(n)))
eta = 1+2.2*x1+3.1*x2
y = exp(rnorm(n, mean = eta,  sd = 1))
data = data.frame(y, x1, x2)
formula=y ~1+x1+x2
r=inla(formula, family ="lognormal", data=data)
summary(r)

When you run this you get three posterior average estimates (intercept and the estimates for the effects of x1 and x2):

> r$summary.fixed$mean
[1] 0.9443243 2.1517555 3.0380717

Now, please correct or improve anything below

I was looking at the pdf of the lognormal and saw eta = mu, so maybe i am going at this completely the wrong way....

Anyway, for the intercept, I would instinctively do the same as if I had log-transformed the response and go with:
> exp(r$summary.fixed$mean[1])
[1] 2.571076
"The overall average of y is 2.57 for x1 = x2 = 0" (wording it better for x1 = x2 = 0 according to what those variable are)

But for the two fixed effects, I am hesitant with just taking the exponential of the output since the effect is additive on the log scale...

I started with

> exp(r$summary.fixed$mean[2:3])
[1]  8.599943 20.864971
"For each one unit increase in x1, y would increase on average by 8.60 , with the effect of x1 remaining constant"
(same kind of thing for x2)

but then it was not sitting quite right. So I was thinking maybe

> (exp(r$summary.fixed$mean[2:3])-1)*100
[1]  759.9943 1986.4971
"For each one unit increase in x1, the average y increases by 759.99%,  with the effect of x1 remaining constant"
(same kind of thing for x2)

I am probably overthinking this. Again my apologies, but after spending 4.5 hours in books and on google, I could not find a final straight answer.

Thank you very much for your help.

Sab.

messages.subject_clean: Error in inla.check.location, Locations are too close
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA users,

I am trying to fit an additive regression model (using the reproducible example below)

y_i ~ Poisson(mu_i), where mu_i = exp(alpha), alpha = {f1(x1) + f2(x2) + f3(x3)}/6

but gets the following error

Error in inla.check.location(location[[r]], term = gp$random.spec[[r]]$term,  :
  Locations are too close for f(x1, model="rw2", ...):  min(diff(sort(x)))/diff(range(x)) = 7.453e-09 < 1e-03
  You can fix this by some kind of binning, see ?inla.group
  If you want/need to bypass this check at your own risk, do
    > m = get("inla.models", INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv())
    > m$latent$rw2$min.diff = NULL
    > assign("inla.models", m, INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv())

The same error occurs also for exponential and binary distributions, and also if I try any of the predictors x1, x2 or x3. On Fri, 2018-08-10 at 00:39 -0700, s.p....@gmail.com wrote:
> I have a question about the correct interpretation of the estimates
> provided by R-INLA when running a LogNormal regression. This is
> probably trivial for everyone on this forum but I am looking for the
> exact proper wording to go with it and how it would differ from
> running a normal regression of log-transform response.
>
> Here is a slight extension of example code form this website, with an
> additional fixed effect:
>
> require(INLA)
> n = 300
> x1 = c(scale(runif(n)))
> x2 = c(scale(runif(n)))
> eta = 1+2.2*x1+3.1*x2
> y = exp(rnorm(n, mean = eta,  sd = 1))
> data = data.frame(y, x1, x2)
> formula=y ~1+x1+x2
> r=inla(formula, family ="lognormal", data=data)
> summary(r)
>
> When you run this you get three posterior average estimates
> (intercept and the estimates for the effects of x1 and x2):
>
> > r$summary.fixed$mean
> [1] 0.9443243 2.1517555 3.0380717

this seems correct.

> I was looking at the pdf of the lognormal and saw eta = mu, so maybe
> i am going at this completely the wrong way....
>
> Anyway, for the intercept, I would instinctively do the same as if I
> had log-transformed the response and go with:

this should be the same as above (up to the default prior for the log
precision, which I havn't checked).

data = data.frame(y, x1, x2)

formula=log(y) ~1+x1+x2
r=inla(formula, family ="normal", data=data)
summary(r)

> > exp(r$summary.fixed$mean[1])
> [1] 2.571076
> "The overall average of y is 2.57 for x1 = x2 = 0" (wording it better
> for x1 = x2 = 0 according to what those variable are)

its not strictly true, as the mean of y depends on also on the
variance. you can say that for log(y) the overall effect is 0.9443243

as you see above, using

y ~ ....

and lognormal, is eqv with

log(y) ~ ...

and normal.

it is not more difficult that this.

messages.subject_clean: unexpected behaviour when changing pc.prec priors in rw2
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am in need of some guidance:

I am trying to follow the example of Lombardoet al 2017 <https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.08513> to model a point pattern with several covariates and (possibly) a spatial random field. The workflow on the paper is as follows:

1 – Include all the covariates in the model as linear effects

2 – Add to model in 1 all covariates as rw (they do rw1, I am doing rw2), evaluate the relationship of the covariates to the point pattern to decide which can stay as linear and which need the non-linear effect.

3 – Model 2 again but only the covariates that have a non-linear relationship with the pattern have a rw effect, the rest stay only as linear

4 – Add a structured spatial effect and check if it improves the performance of the model.

Currently, I am stuck at step 2, having problems with the priors to the rw2 effects, as usual.

load("inla_modelling_data.Rdata")

My covariates are in the dataframe "covars" (including a covariate named b0, which is all 1, that will be the intercept), scaled to mean 0 and sd 1. I add to the dataframe the same covariates but grouped for the rw in step 2:

covars$ChlA_GradientLEV <- inla.group(covars$ChlA_Gradient, n = 20)

covars$colony_distLEV <- inla.group(covars$colony_dist, n = 20)

covars$current_angleLEV <- inla.group(covars$current_angle, n = 20)

covars$current_strengthLEV <- inla.group(covars$current_strength, n = 20)

covars$distance_coastLEV <- inla.group(covars$distance_coast, n = 20)

covars$Ekman_TransportLEV <- inla.group(covars$Ekman_Transport, n = 20)

covars$mixed_layer_thicknessLEV <- inla.group(covars$mixed_layer_thickness, n = 20)

covars$salinityLEV <- inla.group(covars$salinity, n = 20)

covars$slopeLEV <- inla.group(covars$slope, n = 20)

covars$SSTLEV <- inla.group(covars$SST, n = 20)

covars$SST_AnomalyLEV <- inla.group(covars$SST_Anomaly, n = 20)

covars$SST_GradientLEV <- inla.group(covars$SST_Gradient, n = 20)

My response variable is constructed following the example in the spde tutorial:

# 4.1 calculate weights for each node ####

dmesh <- inla.mesh.dual(mesh)

# number of meshnodes and number of datapoints

(nv <- mesh$n)

(n <- nrow(ds.df))

# calculate weights for each meshnode depending on whether they are inside or outside the boundary

sum(w <- sapply(1:length(dmesh), function(i) {

  if (gIntersects(dmesh[i,], bound))

    return(gArea(gIntersection(dmesh[i,], bound)))

  else return(0)

}))

table(w > 0) # false = nodes with weight 0 (outside the boundary)/true = nodes with some weight (inside the boundary)

# 4.2 Construct response vector ####

length(y.pp <- rep(0:1, c(nv, n))) # response (0 for all meshnodes, 1 for all data points)

summary(y.pp) # all 0 and 1

# expected (weights at each mesh node and 0 for all data points)

length(e.pp <- c(w, rep(0, n)))

summary(e.pp) # different values

The stack with the data is created with the following code (A-matrix is 1 because there is no spatial effect so far):

stack.non_spat <- inla.stack(data = list(y = y.pp, e = e.pp),

                             A = list(1),

                             effects = list(covars))

And with the following code I run model 1 (all covars are linear):

# formula

frm.linear <- y ~ -1 + b0 + ChlA_Gradient + colony_dist + current_angle + current_strength + distance_coast + Ekman_Transport + mixed_layer_thickness + salinity + slope + SST + SST_Anomaly + SST_Gradient

# run model

linear.model <- inla(frm.linear,

                     family = "poisson",

                     data = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat),

                     control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack.non_spat), compute = TRUE),

                     E = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat)$e,

                     control.compute = list(dic = F, waic = F, config = T),

                     control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"),

                     verbose = T)

So far, so good, the model runs in about 2.5 seconds, and these are the coefficients I get:

fxd.effects <- cbind(rownames(linear.model$summary.fixed), linear.model$summary.fixed)

names(fxd.effects) <- c("effect", "mean", "sd", "infCI", "median", "supCI", "mode", "kld")

fxd.effects <- fxd.effects[2:13,]

mean_sd <- ggplot(fxd.effects, aes(x = effect, y = mean)) + ylim(-1.7, 1.7) +

  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), width = 0.1) +

  geom_line() +

  geom_point() +

  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + ggtitle("linear")

median_IC <- ggplot(fxd.effects, aes(x = effect, y = median)) + ylim(-1.7, 1.7) +

  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = infCI , ymax = supCI), width = 0.1) +

  geom_line() +

  geom_point() +

  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + ggtitle("linear")

grid.arrange(mean_sd, median_IC, nrow = 2)

The coefficients suggest that some covariates might have much more effect than others in our pattern, and a couple of them have coefficients with CI overlapping 0 suggesting they might not be having an effect. However, from previous exploration of data I know that they do have an effect, and they have very non-linear relationships that are not being captured here.

If we predict from this model using inla.posterior.sample and following the example in https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic112.html :

# Generate posterior sample

psample <- inla.posterior.sample(n = 1000, result = linear.model, use.improved.mean = T)

# Explore contents of the model

contents <-  linear.model$misc$configs$contents

# select from what part of the output we’re going to extract the posterior, in this case, the predictor

effect <-  "Predictor"

id.effect <-  which(contents$tag == effect) # - the numerical id of the effect

ind.effect <-  contents$start[id.effect] - 1 + (1:contents$length[id.effect]) # - all the indices for the effect

# extract the sample from sp_rdm from the posterior sample

sp_sample <-  lapply(psample, function(x) x$latent[ind.effect])

sp_sample <-  matrix(unlist(sp_sample), byrow = T, nrow = 1000)

sp_sample <- exp(sp_sample) #??? exp because log link means i have to backtransform

mean_sp_post <- (colMeans(sp_sample))[1:1098]

sd_sp_post <- (colSds(sp_sample))[1:1098]

proj = inla.mesh.projector(mesh,

                           xlim = poly.barrier@bbox[1,], ylim = poly.barrier@bbox[2,],

                           dims = c(280, 245)) # this is the dimensions of the covars rasters/10. For definitive plots make with more resolution

# project and plot

my.levelplot <-

  function(proj, values,

           col.regions = gray.colors(64, 1, 0),

           aspect = "fill",

           contour = TRUE, labels = FALSE,

           xlim = range(proj$x), ylim = range(proj$y),

           poly = poly.barrier,

           ...) {

    z = inla.mesh.project(proj, values)

   return(levelplot(

      row.values = proj$x, column.values = proj$y, x = z,

      xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim,

      col.regions = col.regions, aspect = aspect,

      contour = contour, labels = labels, ...))

  }

psample.mean <- my.levelplot(proj, mean_sp_post, col.regions = plasma(20),

                             main = "Posterior mean", xlab = "", ylab = "")

psample.mean <- psample.mean + latticeExtra::layer(sp.polygons(poly.barrier, lwd = 1, fill = "gray")) +

  latticeExtra::layer(sp.points(ds.df, pch = ".", col = "white", alpha = 0.5))

psample.sd <http://psample.sd> <- my.levelplot(proj, sd_sp_post, col.regions = plasma(20),

                           main = "Posterior sd", xlab = "", ylab = "")

psample.sd <http://psample.sd> <- psample.sd <http://psample.sd> + latticeExtra::layer(sp.polygons(poly.barrier, lwd = 1, fill = "gray"))

grid.arrange(psample.mean, psample.sd <http://psample.sd>, ncol = 2)

These results make sense(ish), although, as expected, the “prediction” is not quite good. So, let’s add the covariates as rw2 (step 2) and see what happens:

# formula

frm.rw <http://frm.rw> <- y ~ -1 + b0 + ChlA_Gradient + colony_dist + current_angle + current_strength + distance_coast + Ekman_Transport + mixed_layer_thickness + salinity + slope + SST + SST_Anomaly + SST_Gradient +

  f(ChlA_GradientLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(colony_distLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(slopeLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(current_angleLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(current_strengthLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(distance_coastLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(Ekman_TransportLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(mixed_layer_thicknessLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(salinityLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(SSTLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(SST_AnomalyLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

  f(SST_GradientLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01))))

If I understood the documentation about pc.prec correctly, the smaller the <u> parameter, the less “wiggly” the rw will be (less overfitting). I start by using <u> = 1 and <alpha> = 0.01 to begin with, to see what happens:

non.linear.model <- inla(frm.rw <http://frm.rw>,

                         family = "poisson",

                         data = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat),

                         control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack.non_spat), compute = TRUE, link = 1),

                         E = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat)$e,

                         control.compute = list(dic = F, waic = F, config = T),

                         control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"),

                         verbose = T)

while running, I see a lot of

“Variable evaluates to NAN or INF. I will try to fix it...

but the model runs successfully nonetheless in about  half an hour.

Using the same code as above to extract coefficients for the linear terms, and plotting them next to those of the only linear model, we get this:

Values and even signs for the coefficients have changed as the non-linear effects do a better job of capturing the structure of the pattern. But still, all coefficients are within "normal" values. If we plot these non-linear effects:

messages.body_plain:
Hi Virginia,

There were many questions here, let me focus on the wigglyness of "rw2" and others pitch in on the other questions.

The wigglyness of rw2 is determined by the hyper-parameter in a way, yes. The problem with this is that both the size of the effect and the wigglyness are determined by the same parameter. So if you "shrink" the wigglyness, you also "shrink" the size of the random effect.

The wigglyness of rw2 is also determined by the number of groups you use in inla.group. In theory, it should not be. In theory the groups should be so many that the model specification (including priors) give the same thing no matter how many groups you use. In theory.

In practice, however, what many do is they have few groups (say 10) so that the rw2 components does not overfit too much. This would be similar to having just a few basis-splines in a b/p/... spline model. This is not a great solution from a statistical point of view (as we are making "unfounded/magical" modeling assumptions).

PS: The main question I would make about your model is whether it is identifiable. If the data was truly from this model, would you be able to recover the structure and estimate the parameters?

Kind regards,
Haakon

Thanks for your suggestion on rw "wigglyness", it was very useful! (I've decided to focus on practicality for the time being, keeping in mind that just reducing the number of groups is not the optimal solution from a statistical point of view). I've modified the model a bit, removed some covariates, and everything seems to be making much more sense, the effects of the covariates have the shape I'd expect them to have. However, when trying to predict using inla.postierior.sample I still get the weird very flat surface all over the study area with one location with a very high intensity (although now the very high intensity location has moved).

It looks to me as if there's something going on that doesn't have to do with my data or covariates, but rather with what happens "behind the scenes". It looks very similar to what happened here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/BJA9pguPROU> when I was trying a similar model with inlabru, which is the reason why I ended up moving to INLA. I'll try to go over the solutions Finn and you offered at that moment, and see if I can detect what's going wrong.

What I would like to know at this point, though, is whether that means I can't trust the results on effects of my covariates either or if it is just the posterior sampling that's going wrong...

Thanks again for the help!

Virginia Morera-Pujol
PhD Student
BEECA
University of Barcelona

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
the inlabru code for constructing the lgcp likelihood has changed since you tried it,
partly to fix some instabilities in the integration scheme, and it’s possible you’re
encountering related issues in the method you’re using now. It’s essential for the
Poisson process likelihood approximation to have positive integration weights on the vertices of
any and all triangle in which there are observed points. If any point lies in a triangle
that doesn’t have nonzero integration weights, then I’d expect to see problems of this type.

Finn

> > The wigglyness of rw2 is determined by the hyper-parameter in a way, yes. The problem with this is that both the size of the effect and the wigglyness are determined by the same parameter. So if you "shrink" the wigglyness, you also "shrink" the size of the random effect.
> >
> > The wigglyness of rw2 is also determined by the number of groups you use in inla.group. In theory, it should not be. In theory the groups should be so many that the model specification (including priors) give the same thing no matter how many groups you use. In theory.
> >
> > In practice, however, what many do is they have few groups (say 10) so that the rw2 components does not overfit too much. This would be similar to having just a few basis-splines in a b/p/... spline model. This is not a great solution from a statistical point of view (as we are making "unfounded/magical" modeling assumptions).

> > >

> > >
> > > So far, so good, the model runs in about 2.5 seconds, and these are the coefficients I get:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > fxd.effects <- cbind(rownames(linear.model$summary.fixed), linear.model$summary.fixed)
> > >
> > > names(fxd.effects) <- c("effect", "mean", "sd", "infCI", "median", "supCI", "mode", "kld")

However, from previous exploration of data I know that they do have an effect, and they have very non-linear relationships that are not being captured here.
> > >

> > >
> > >

> > >
> > > effect <-  "Predictor"
> > >
> > > id.effect <-  which(contents$tag == effect) # - the numerical id of the effect
> > >
> > > ind.effect <-  contents$start[id.effect] - 1 + (1:contents$length[id.effect]) # - all the indices for the effect
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > # extract the sample from sp_rdm from the posterior sample
> > >
> > > sp_sample <-  lapply(psample, function(x) x$latent[ind.effect])
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > sp_sample <-  matrix(unlist(sp_sample), byrow = T, nrow = 1000)
> > >
> > >
> > >

> > >

> > > These results make sense(ish), although, as expected, the “prediction” is not quite good. So, let’s add the covariates as rw2 (step 2) and see what happens:

> > >

> > >
> > >   f(distance_coastLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > >

> > >
> > >   f(mixed_layer_thicknessLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +

> > >
> > >   f(SSTLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > >
> > >   f(SST_AnomalyLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > >
> > >   f(SST_GradientLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01))))
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > If I understood the documentation about pc.prec correctly, the smaller the <u> parameter, the less “wiggly” the rw will be (less overfitting). I start by using <u> = 1 and <alpha> = 0.01 to begin with, to see what happens:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > non.linear.model <- inla(frm.rw <http://frm.rw>,
> > >
> > >                          family = "poisson",
> > >
> > >                          data = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat),
> > >
> > >                          control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack.non_spat), compute = TRUE, link = 1),
> > >
> > >                          E = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat)$e,
> > >
> > >                          control.compute = list(dic = F, waic = F, config = T),
> > >
> > >                          control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"),
> > >

> > >

> > > while running, I see a lot of
> > >
> > > “Variable evaluates to NAN or INF. I will try to fix it...

> > > but the model runs successfully nonetheless in about  half an hour.
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Using the same code as above to extract coefficients for the linear terms, and plotting them next to those of the only linear model, we get this:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > Values and even signs for the coefficients have changed as the non-linear effects do a better job of capturing the structure of the pattern. But still, all coefficients are within "normal" values. If we plot these non-linear effects:
> > >
> > >
> > >
> > > par(mfrow = c(4,3), mar = c(3,3,1,0.3), mgp = c(2,1,0))
> > >
> > > for (i in seq_along(names(non.linear.model$summary.random))) {
> > >
> > >   # i = 1
> > >
> > >   cov_name <- substr(names(non.linear.model$summary.random)[i], 1, nchar(names(non.linear.model$summary.random)[i]) - 3)
> > >
> > >   scaled_vals <- cov_list[[cov_name]]

> > >

If I run the same model but with param = c(0.5, 0.01) for the “pc.prec” of all the covariates,but here start the problems: to begin with, coefficients for the linear effects take on seemingly unreasonable values (beware of different scales of y axes for linear and non-linear).
> > >
> > >
> > > Non-linear effects also have extreme values:
> > >
> > >

> > >
> > >

This has happened before while trying to run a model with similar data but only one covariate + a spatial effect with inlabru, and Finn suggested this was due to instabilities in the prediction function of the inlabru package (or so I understood from what he said) which is why I switched back to inla... Is it possible that something similar is happening here? Or am I doing something wrong (as usual)?

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In rare cases, this can also be a phenomenon in the data itself. If you have a very tight cluster of points, and an exponential link function, this "single hotspot(s)" can be a feature of your data. If you plot the results on log scale you will see less marked differences between the hotspot and the flat area.

Kind regards,
Haakon

On 14 August 2018 at 21:22, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
> the inlabru code for constructing the lgcp likelihood has changed since you tried it,
> partly to fix some instabilities in the integration scheme, and it’s possible you’re
> encountering related issues in the method you’re using now. It’s essential for the
> Poisson process likelihood approximation to have positive integration weights on the vertices of
> any and all triangle in which there are observed points. If any point lies in a triangle

> that doesn’t have nonzero integration weights, then I’d expect to see problems of this type.
>
> Finn
>
> On 14 Aug 2018, at 18:23, Virginia Morera Pujol <morera....@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> > Hi Haakon,
> >
> > Thanks for your suggestion on rw "wigglyness", it was very useful! (I've decided to focus on practicality for the time being, keeping in mind that just reducing the number of groups is not the optimal solution from a statistical point of view). I've modified the model a bit, removed some covariates, and everything seems to be making much more sense, the effects of the covariates have the shape I'd expect them to have. However, when trying to predict using inla.postierior.sample I still get the weird very flat surface all over the study area with one location with a very high intensity (although now the very high intensity location has moved).
> > <imagen.png>
> >
> > It looks to me as if there's something going on that doesn't have to do with my data or covariates, but rather with what happens "behind the scenes". It looks very similar to what happened here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/BJA9pguPROU> when I was trying a similar model with inlabru, which is the reason why I ended up moving to INLA. I'll try to go over the solutions Finn and you offered at that moment, and see if I can detect what's going wrong.
> >
> > What I would like to know at this point, though, is whether that means I can't trust the results on effects of my covariates either or if it is just the posterior sampling that's going wrong...
> >
> > Thanks again for the help!
> >
> > Virginia Morera-Pujol
> > PhD Student
> > BEECA
> > University of Barcelona
> >

> > On Tue, 14 Aug 2018 at 12:11, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:

> > > Hi Virginia,
> > >
> > > There were many questions here, let me focus on the wigglyness of "rw2" and others pitch in on the other questions.
> > >
> > > The wigglyness of rw2 is determined by the hyper-parameter in a way, yes. The problem with this is that both the size of the effect and the wigglyness are determined by the same parameter. So if you "shrink" the wigglyness, you also "shrink" the size of the random effect.
> > >
> > > The wigglyness of rw2 is also determined by the number of groups you use in inla.group. In theory, it should not be. In theory the groups should be so many that the model specification (including priors) give the same thing no matter how many groups you use. In theory.
> > >
> > > In practice, however, what many do is they have few groups (say 10) so that the rw2 components does not overfit too much. This would be similar to having just a few basis-splines in a b/p/... spline model. This is not a great solution from a statistical point of view (as we are making "unfounded/magical" modeling assumptions).
> > >
> > > PS: The main question I would make about your model is whether it is identifiable. If the data was truly from this model, would you be able to recover the structure and estimate the parameters?
> > >
> > >
> > > Kind regards,
> > > Haakon
> > >
> > >
> > >

> > > On 13 August 2018 at 18:19, Virginia Morera Pujol <morera....@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > # 4.2 Construct response vector ####

> > > > length(y.pp <- rep(0:1, c(nv, n))) # response (0 for all meshnodes, 1 for all data points)

> > > >
> > > > The stack with the data is created with the following code (A-matrix is 1 because there is no spatial effect so far):

> > > >
> > > > And with the following code I run model 1 (all covars are linear):
> > > >

> > > > # formula
> > > >
> > > > frm.linear <- y ~ -1 + b0 + ChlA_Gradient + colony_dist + current_angle + current_strength + distance_coast + Ekman_Transport + mixed_layer_thickness + salinity + slope + SST + SST_Anomaly + SST_Gradient
> > > >

> > > > So far, so good, the model runs in about 2.5 seconds, and these are the coefficients I get:

> > > >

messages.body_plain:
Ok, thanks to both of you! I might try to give it another go in the latest version of inlabru then. However, with the model as it is now:

1) I do have 0 weight integration points, but all of them in the outside boundary (following the script on the SPDE tutorial). In the image, all points in red have 0 weight, and the light blue line delimits the inner boundary

I guess since the inla.posterior.sample is using all the mesh, inner and outer boundary, this might be causing a problem? Is there a way I can tell the function to sample only in the inner boundary?

2) I do have very clustered points. Or rather, very clustered points in relation to very large very empty regions in my study area. I defined my inner boundary based on the convex hull of my points, on the principle that it would cover the area where my animals could have gone but decided not to (my points are animal locations).

This means that there are large empty areas, which leaves the rest of the locations looking very clustered indeed. I can think of two solutions for this: first, I thin my point pattern further, until I remove the very strong clustering. But this clustering is what I want to model (or rather, figure out what is causing it), so it doesn't make sense that I get rid of it! Second, I reshape my boundary to fit it more "tightly" to my points. However, it seems to me that I would be depriving the model of important information such as the values of the covariates in the location where the animals don't go, which to me seems rather important from an ecological point of view... Is there any other way to solve this?

Regards,

Virginia Morera-Pujol
PhD Student
BEECA
University of Barcelona

On Tue, 14 Aug 2018 at 20:51, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> In rare cases, this can also be a phenomenon in the data itself. If you have a very tight cluster of points, and an exponential link function, this "single hotspot(s)" can be a feature of your data. If you plot the results on log scale you will see less marked differences between the hotspot and the flat area.
>
> Kind regards,
> Haakon

> On 14 August 2018 at 21:22, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Hi,
> > the inlabru code for constructing the lgcp likelihood has changed since you tried it,
> > partly to fix some instabilities in the integration scheme, and it’s possible you’re
> > encountering related issues in the method you’re using now. It’s essential for the
> > Poisson process likelihood approximation to have positive integration weights on the vertices of
> > any and all triangle in which there are observed points. If any point lies in a triangle

> > that doesn’t have nonzero integration weights, then I’d expect to see problems of this type.
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > On 14 Aug 2018, at 18:23, Virginia Morera Pujol <morera....@gmail.com> wrote:
> >

> > > Hi Haakon,
> > >
> > > Thanks for your suggestion on rw "wigglyness", it was very useful! (I've decided to focus on practicality for the time being, keeping in mind that just reducing the number of groups is not the optimal solution from a statistical point of view). I've modified the model a bit, removed some covariates, and everything seems to be making much more sense, the effects of the covariates have the shape I'd expect them to have. However, when trying to predict using inla.postierior.sample I still get the weird very flat surface all over the study area with one location with a very high intensity (although now the very high intensity location has moved).
> > > <imagen.png>
> > >
> > > It looks to me as if there's something going on that doesn't have to do with my data or covariates, but rather with what happens "behind the scenes". It looks very similar to what happened here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/BJA9pguPROU> when I was trying a similar model with inlabru, which is the reason why I ended up moving to INLA. I'll try to go over the solutions Finn and you offered at that moment, and see if I can detect what's going wrong.
> > >
> > > What I would like to know at this point, though, is whether that means I can't trust the results on effects of my covariates either or if it is just the posterior sampling that's going wrong...
> > >
> > > Thanks again for the help!
> > >
> > > Virginia Morera-Pujol
> > > PhD Student
> > > BEECA
> > > University of Barcelona
> > >

> > > On Tue, 14 Aug 2018 at 12:11, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:

> > > > Hi Virginia,
> > > >
> > > > There were many questions here, let me focus on the wigglyness of "rw2" and others pitch in on the other questions.
> > > >
> > > > The wigglyness of rw2 is determined by the hyper-parameter in a way, yes. The problem with this is that both the size of the effect and the wigglyness are determined by the same parameter. So if you "shrink" the wigglyness, you also "shrink" the size of the random effect.
> > > >
> > > > The wigglyness of rw2 is also determined by the number of groups you use in inla.group. In theory, it should not be. In theory the groups should be so many that the model specification (including priors) give the same thing no matter how many groups you use. In theory.
> > > >
> > > > In practice, however, what many do is they have few groups (say 10) so that the rw2 components does not overfit too much. This would be similar to having just a few basis-splines in a b/p/... spline model. This is not a great solution from a statistical point of view (as we are making "unfounded/magical" modeling assumptions).
> > > >
> > > > PS: The main question I would make about your model is whether it is identifiable. If the data was truly from this model, would you be able to recover the structure and estimate the parameters?
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > Kind regards,
> > > > Haakon
> > > >
> > > >

On 15 Aug 2018, at 08:51, Virginia Morera Pujol <morera....@gmail.com> wrote:

> Ok, thanks to both of you! I might try to give it another go in the latest version of inlabru then. However, with the model as it is now:
>
> 1) I do have 0 weight integration points, but all of them in the outside boundary (following the script on the SPDE tutorial). In the image, all points in red have 0 weight, and the light blue line delimits the inner boundary

> <imagen.png>
> I guess since the inla.posterior.sample is using all the mesh, inner and outer boundary, this might be causing a problem? Is there a way I can tell the function to sample only in the inner boundary?
>
> 2) I do have very clustered points. Or rather, very clustered points in relation to very large very empty regions in my study area. I defined my inner boundary based on the convex hull of my points, on the principle that it would cover the area where my animals could have gone but decided not to (my points are animal locations).

> <imagen.png>
> This means that there are large empty areas, which leaves the rest of the locations looking very clustered indeed. I can think of two solutions for this: first, I thin my point pattern further, until I remove the very strong clustering. But this clustering is what I want to model (or rather, figure out what is causing it), so it doesn't make sense that I get rid of it! Second, I reshape my boundary to fit it more "tightly" to my points. However, it seems to me that I would be depriving the model of important information such as the values of the covariates in the location where the animals don't go, which to me seems rather important from an ecological point of view... Is there any other way to solve this?
>
>
> Regards,
> Virginia Morera-Pujol
> PhD Student
> BEECA
> University of Barcelona
>

>
> On Tue, 14 Aug 2018 at 20:51, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > In rare cases, this can also be a phenomenon in the data itself. If you have a very tight cluster of points, and an exponential link function, this "single hotspot(s)" can be a feature of your data. If you plot the results on log scale you will see less marked differences between the hotspot and the flat area.
> >
> > Kind regards,
> > Haakon
> >
> > On 14 August 2018 at 21:22, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi,
> > > the inlabru code for constructing the lgcp likelihood has changed since you tried it,
> > > partly to fix some instabilities in the integration scheme, and it’s possible you’re
> > > encountering related issues in the method you’re using now. It’s essential for the
> > > Poisson process likelihood approximation to have positive integration weights on the vertices of
> > > any and all triangle in which there are observed points. If any point lies in a triangle
> > > that doesn’t have nonzero integration weights, then I’d expect to see problems of this type.
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > > On 14 Aug 2018, at 18:23, Virginia Morera Pujol <morera....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > > Hi Haakon,

(I've decided to focus on practicality for the time being, keeping in mind that just reducing the number of groups is not the optimal solution from a statistical point of view). However, when trying to predict using inla.postierior.sample I still get the weird very flat surface all over the study area with one location with a very high intensity (although now the very high intensity location has moved).
> > > > <imagen.png>
> > > >

It looks very similar to what happened here <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/r-inla-discussion-group/BJA9pguPROU> when I was trying a similar model with inlabru, which is the reason why I ended up moving to INLA. I'll try to go over the solutions Finn and you offered at that moment, and see if I can detect what's going wrong.
> > > >
> > > > What I would like to know at this point, though, is whether that means I can't trust the results on effects of my covariates either or if it is just the posterior sampling that's going wrong...
> > > >
> > > > Thanks again for the help!
> > > >
> > > > Virginia Morera-Pujol
> > > > PhD Student
> > > > BEECA
> > > > University of Barcelona

> > > > On Tue, 14 Aug 2018 at 12:11, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:
> > > > > Hi Virginia,
> > > > >
> > > > > There were many questions here, let me focus on the wigglyness of "rw2" and others pitch in on the other questions.
> > > > >
> > > > > The wigglyness of rw2 is determined by the hyper-parameter in a way, yes. The problem with this is that both the size of the effect and the wigglyness are determined by the same parameter. So if you "shrink" the wigglyness, you also "shrink" the size of the random effect.
> > > > >
> > > > > The wigglyness of rw2 is also determined by the number of groups you use in inla.group. In theory, it should not be. In theory the groups should be so many that the model specification (including priors) give the same thing no matter how many groups you use. In theory.
> > > > >
> > > > > In practice, however, what many do is they have few groups (say 10) so that the rw2 components does not overfit too much. This would be similar to having just a few basis-splines in a b/p/... spline model. This is not a great solution from a statistical point of view (as we are making "unfounded/magical" modeling assumptions).
> > > > >
> > > > > PS: The main question I would make about your model is whether it is identifiable. If the data was truly from this model, would you be able to recover the structure and estimate the parameters?

> > > > >

> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > My covariates are in the dataframe "covars" (including a covariate named b0, which is all 1, that will be the intercept), scaled to mean 0 and sd 1. I add to the dataframe the same covariates but grouped for the rw in step 2:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$ChlA_GradientLEV <- inla.group(covars$ChlA_Gradient, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$colony_distLEV <- inla.group(covars$colony_dist, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$current_angleLEV <- inla.group(covars$current_angle, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$current_strengthLEV <- inla.group(covars$current_strength, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$distance_coastLEV <- inla.group(covars$distance_coast, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$Ekman_TransportLEV <- inla.group(covars$Ekman_Transport, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$mixed_layer_thicknessLEV <- inla.group(covars$mixed_layer_thickness, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$salinityLEV <- inla.group(covars$salinity, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$slopeLEV <- inla.group(covars$slope, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$SSTLEV <- inla.group(covars$SST, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$SST_AnomalyLEV <- inla.group(covars$SST_Anomaly, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > covars$SST_GradientLEV <- inla.group(covars$SST_Gradient, n = 20)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > My response variable is constructed following the example in the spde tutorial:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # 4.1 calculate weights for each node ####
> > > > > >
> > > > > > dmesh <- inla.mesh.dual(mesh)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # number of meshnodes and number of datapoints
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (nv <- mesh$n)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > (n <- nrow(ds.df))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # calculate weights for each meshnode depending on whether they are inside or outside the boundary
> > > > > >
> > > > > > sum(w <- sapply(1:length(dmesh), function(i) {
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   if (gIntersects(dmesh[i,], bound))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >     return(gArea(gIntersection(dmesh[i,], bound)))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   else return(0)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > }))
> > > > > >
> > > > > > table(w > 0) # false = nodes with weight 0 (outside the boundary)/true = nodes with some weight (inside the boundary)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # 4.2 Construct response vector ####
> > > > > >
> > > > > > length(y.pp <- rep(0:1, c(nv, n))) # response (0 for all meshnodes, 1 for all data points)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > summary(y.pp) # all 0 and 1
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # expected (weights at each mesh node and 0 for all data points)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > length(e.pp <- c(w, rep(0, n)))
> > > > > >
> > > > > > summary(e.pp) # different values
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The stack with the data is created with the following code (A-matrix is 1 because there is no spatial effect so far):
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > stack.non_spat <- inla.stack(data = list(y = y.pp, e = e.pp),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                              A = list(1),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                              effects = list(covars))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > And with the following code I run model 1 (all covars are linear):
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # formula
> > > > > >
> > > > > > frm.linear <- y ~ -1 + b0 + ChlA_Gradient + colony_dist + current_angle + current_strength + distance_coast + Ekman_Transport + mixed_layer_thickness + salinity + slope + SST + SST_Anomaly + SST_Gradient
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # run model
> > > > > >
> > > > > > linear.model <- inla(frm.linear,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                      family = "poisson",
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                      data = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                      control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack.non_spat), compute = TRUE),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                      E = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat)$e,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                      control.compute = list(dic = F, waic = F, config = T),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                      control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                      verbose = T)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > So far, so good, the model runs in about 2.5 seconds, and these are the coefficients I get:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > fxd.effects <- cbind(rownames(linear.model$summary.fixed), linear.model$summary.fixed)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > names(fxd.effects) <- c("effect", "mean", "sd", "infCI", "median", "supCI", "mode", "kld")
> > > > > >
> > > > > > fxd.effects <- fxd.effects[2:13,]
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > mean_sd <- ggplot(fxd.effects, aes(x = effect, y = mean)) + ylim(-1.7, 1.7) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean - sd, ymax = mean + sd), width = 0.1) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   geom_line() +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   geom_point() +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + ggtitle("linear")
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > median_IC <- ggplot(fxd.effects, aes(x = effect, y = median)) + ylim(-1.7, 1.7) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = infCI , ymax = supCI), width = 0.1) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   geom_line() +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   geom_point() +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + ggtitle("linear")
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > grid.arrange(mean_sd, median_IC, nrow = 2)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The coefficients suggest that some covariates might have much more effect than others in our pattern, and a couple of them have coefficients with CI overlapping 0 suggesting they might not be having an effect. However, from previous exploration of data I know that they do have an effect, and they have very non-linear relationships that are not being captured here.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If we predict from this model using inla.posterior.sample and following the example in https://haakonbakka.bitbucket.io/btopic112.html :
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # Generate posterior sample
> > > > > >
> > > > > > psample <- inla.posterior.sample(n = 1000, result = linear.model, use.improved.mean = T)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # Explore contents of the model
> > > > > >
> > > > > > contents <-  linear.model$misc$configs$contents
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # select from what part of the output we’re going to extract the posterior, in this case, the predictor
> > > > > >
> > > > > > effect <-  "Predictor"
> > > > > >
> > > > > > id.effect <-  which(contents$tag == effect) # - the numerical id of the effect
> > > > > >
> > > > > > ind.effect <-  contents$start[id.effect] - 1 + (1:contents$length[id.effect]) # - all the indices for the effect
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # extract the sample from sp_rdm from the posterior sample
> > > > > >
> > > > > > sp_sample <-  lapply(psample, function(x) x$latent[ind.effect])
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > sp_sample <-  matrix(unlist(sp_sample), byrow = T, nrow = 1000)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > sp_sample <- exp(sp_sample) #??? exp because log link means i have to backtransform
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > mean_sp_post <- (colMeans(sp_sample))[1:1098]
> > > > > >
> > > > > > sd_sp_post <- (colSds(sp_sample))[1:1098]
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > proj = inla.mesh.projector(mesh,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                            xlim = poly.barrier@bbox[1,], ylim = poly.barrier@bbox[2,],
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                            dims = c(280, 245)) # this is the dimensions of the covars rasters/10. For definitive plots make with more resolution
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # project and plot
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > my.levelplot <-
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   function(proj, values,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >            col.regions = gray.colors(64, 1, 0),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >            aspect = "fill",
> > > > > >
> > > > > >            contour = TRUE, labels = FALSE,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >            xlim = range(proj$x), ylim = range(proj$y),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >            poly = poly.barrier,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >            ...) {
> > > > > >
> > > > > >     z = inla.mesh.project(proj, values)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >    return(levelplot(
> > > > > >
> > > > > >       row.values = proj$x, column.values = proj$y, x = z,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >       xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >       col.regions = col.regions, aspect = aspect,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >       contour = contour, labels = labels, ...))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   }
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > psample.mean <- my.levelplot(proj, mean_sp_post, col.regions = plasma(20),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                              main = "Posterior mean", xlab = "", ylab = "")
> > > > > >
> > > > > > psample.mean <- psample.mean + latticeExtra::layer(sp.polygons(poly.barrier, lwd = 1, fill = "gray")) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   latticeExtra::layer(sp.points(ds.df, pch = ".", col = "white", alpha = 0.5))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > psample.sd <http://psample.sd> <- my.levelplot(proj, sd_sp_post, col.regions = plasma(20),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                            main = "Posterior sd", xlab = "", ylab = "")
> > > > > >
> > > > > > psample.sd <http://psample.sd> <- psample.sd <http://psample.sd> + latticeExtra::layer(sp.polygons(poly.barrier, lwd = 1, fill = "gray"))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > grid.arrange(psample.mean, psample.sd <http://psample.sd>, ncol = 2)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > These results make sense(ish), although, as expected, the “prediction” is not quite good. So, let’s add the covariates as rw2 (step 2) and see what happens:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # formula
> > > > > >
> > > > > > frm.rw <http://frm.rw> <- y ~ -1 + b0 + ChlA_Gradient + colony_dist + current_angle + current_strength + distance_coast + Ekman_Transport + mixed_layer_thickness + salinity + slope + SST + SST_Anomaly + SST_Gradient +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(ChlA_GradientLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(colony_distLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(slopeLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(current_angleLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(current_strengthLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(distance_coastLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(Ekman_TransportLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(mixed_layer_thicknessLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(salinityLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(SSTLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(SST_AnomalyLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01)))) +
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   f(SST_GradientLEV, model = 'rw2', scale.model = T, hyper = list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1, 0.01))))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > If I understood the documentation about pc.prec correctly, the smaller the <u> parameter, the less “wiggly” the rw will be (less overfitting). I start by using <u> = 1 and <alpha> = 0.01 to begin with, to see what happens:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > non.linear.model <- inla(frm.rw <http://frm.rw>,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                          family = "poisson",
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                          data = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                          control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack.non_spat), compute = TRUE, link = 1),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                          E = inla.stack.data(stack.non_spat)$e,
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                          control.compute = list(dic = F, waic = F, config = T),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                          control.inla = list(int.strategy = "eb"),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >                          verbose = T)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > while running, I see a lot of
> > > > > >
> > > > > > “Variable evaluates to NAN or INF. I will try to fix it...
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > but the model runs successfully nonetheless in about  half an hour.
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Using the same code as above to extract coefficients for the linear terms, and plotting them next to those of the only linear model, we get this:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Values and even signs for the coefficients have changed as the non-linear effects do a better job of capturing the structure of the pattern. But still, all coefficients are within "normal" values. If we plot these non-linear effects:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > par(mfrow = c(4,3), mar = c(3,3,1,0.3), mgp = c(2,1,0))
> > > > > >
> > > > > > for (i in seq_along(names(non.linear.model$summary.random))) {
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   # i = 1
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   cov_name <- substr(names(non.linear.model$summary.random)[i], 1, nchar(names(non.linear.model$summary.random)[i]) - 3)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   scaled_vals <- cov_list[[cov_name]]
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   unscaled_vals <- scaled_vals*attr(scaled_vals, 'scaled:scale') + attr(scaled_vals, 'scaled:center')
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   plot(non.linear.model$summary.random[[i]][,1:2], type = 'l', xlab = cov_name, ylab = 'Effect', xaxt = "n")
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   axis(side = 1, at = seq(from = min(scaled_vals), to = max(scaled_vals), length = 6),
> > > > > >
> > > > > >        labels = round(seq(from = min(unscaled_vals), to = max(unscaled_vals), length = 6)))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
> > > > > >
> > > > > >   for (j in c(4,6)) {lines(non.linear.model$summary.random[[i]][,c(1,j)], lty = 2) }
> > > > > >
> > > > > > }
> > > > > >
> > > > > > par(mfrow = c(1,1))
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Most of the covariates are “over-fitted” so I should change the prior for the precision. If I run the same model but with param = c(0.5, 0.01) for the “pc.prec” of all the covariates,but here start the problems: to begin with, coefficients for the linear effects take on seemingly unreasonable values (beware of different scales of y axes for linear and non-linear).
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Non-linear effects also have extreme values:
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The same procedure to predict as used above produces the following plots (I have removed the polygon covering the prediction over the outer boundary, so you can see what's going on):
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > All the intensity is concentrated in a specific point of the outer boundary. This has happened before while trying to run a model with similar data but only one covariate + a spatial effect with inlabru, and Finn suggested this was due to instabilities in the prediction function of the inlabru package (or so I understood from what he said) which is why I switched back to inla... Is it possible that something similar is happening here? Or am I doing something wrong (as usual)?
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Data, mesh and covariates are attached
> > > > > >
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Thanks a lot!

messages.body_plain:
You can also try to refine the mesh in the area where you get the spike. To see if the spike is always at just one mesh node, or if it covers several.

On 15 August 2018 at 12:30, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:

> If the artifact is outside the point process domain, ignore it.  Only look at the field inside your domain.
>
> Finn
>
> On 15 Aug 2018, at 08:51, Virginia Morera Pujol <morera....@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> > Ok, thanks to both of you! I might try to give it another go in the latest version of inlabru then. However, with the model as it is now:
> >
> > 1) I do have 0 weight integration points, but all of them in the outside boundary (following the script on the SPDE tutorial). In the image, all points in red have 0 weight, and the light blue line delimits the inner boundary
> > <imagen.png>
> > I guess since the inla.posterior.sample is using all the mesh, inner and outer boundary, this might be causing a problem? Is there a way I can tell the function to sample only in the inner boundary?
> >
> > 2) I do have very clustered points. Or rather, very clustered points in relation to very large very empty regions in my study area. I defined my inner boundary based on the convex hull of my points, on the principle that it would cover the area where my animals could have gone but decided not to (my points are animal locations).
> > <imagen.png>
> > This means that there are large empty areas, which leaves the rest of the locations looking very clustered indeed. I can think of two solutions for this: first, I thin my point pattern further, until I remove the very strong clustering. But this clustering is what I want to model (or rather, figure out what is causing it), so it doesn't make sense that I get rid of it! Second, I reshape my boundary to fit it more "tightly" to my points. However, it seems to me that I would be depriving the model of important information such as the values of the covariates in the location where the animals don't go, which to me seems rather important from an ecological point of view... Is there any other way to solve this?
> >
> >
> > Regards,
> > Virginia Morera-Pujol
> > PhD Student
> > BEECA
> > University of Barcelona
> >

> > On Tue, 14 Aug 2018 at 20:51, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:

> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > In rare cases, this can also be a phenomenon in the data itself. If you have a very tight cluster of points, and an exponential link function, this "single hotspot(s)" can be a feature of your data. If you plot the results on log scale you will see less marked differences between the hotspot and the flat area.
> > >

> > > > > > The wigglyness of rw2 is determined by the hyper-parameter in a way, yes. The problem with this is that both the size of the effect and the wigglyness are determined by the same parameter. So if you "shrink" the wigglyness, you also "shrink" the size of the random effect.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The wigglyness of rw2 is also determined by the number of groups you use in inla.group. In theory, it should not be. In theory the groups should be so many that the model specification (including priors) give the same thing no matter how many groups you use. In theory.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > In practice, however, what many do is they have few groups (say 10) so that the rw2 components does not overfit too much. This would be similar to having just a few basis-splines in a b/p/... spline model. This is not a great solution from a statistical point of view (as we are making "unfounded/magical" modeling assumptions).

> > > > > > PS: The main question I would make about your model is whether it is identifiable. If the data was truly from this model, would you be able to recover the structure and estimate the parameters?
