messages.subject: summary.fitted.values and simulated responses differ
messages.subject_clean: summary.fitted.values and simulated responses differ
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm fitting a negative binomial model with an SPDE and an RW1 random effect, and my summary.fitted.values do not match the results I get when I simulate results from posterior samples.

Here's an example of my summary.fitted.values:

And here is an example of the values I get when taking the mean of 1000 posterior samples, using the following code:

#Create 1000 sets of simulated responses from the model realizations
#sim_nbin_aeg is a matrix holding the 1000 model realizations
#BetaNum_aeg, WeekNum_aeg, SpatialNum_aeg are indices of where the relevant values are in fit$latent
#mat_aeg_sim is a model matrix of the predictors
#mat_aeg_weeks_stemp is an N x 1 matrix of the weeks (for the RW1)

weekFun <- function(weekmatrix, wk) { #This function creates an N x 1 matrix of the coef values for the RW1
  mat = matrix(nrow=N, ncol=1)
  for(i in 1:N) {
    mat[i,]= wk[weekmatrix[i]]
  }
  return(mat)
}

mu.i <- matrix(nrow = N, ncol = Nsim)
Am   <- as.matrix(A)
for (i in 1: Nsim){
  size <- as.numeric(sim_stemp_aeg[[i]]$hyperpar[1])
  Betas     <- sim_stemp_aeg[[i]]$latent[BetaNum_aeg]
  wk        <- sim_stemp_aeg[[i]]$latent[WeekNum_aeg]
  spatials  <- sim_stemp_aeg[[i]]$latent[SpatialNum_aeg]
  FixedPart <- mat_aeg_sim_stemp %*% Betas + Am %*% spatials + weekFun(mat_aeg_weeks_stemp, wk)
  mu.i[,i]  <- exp(FixedPart)
  aeg_stemp_sim[,i] <- rnegbin(n = N,
                              mu = mu.i[,i],
                              theta = size)
}

Have I done something wrong here in how I created the simulated values? I note that the summary.fitted.values has far fewer zeroes and ones, and has a peak at 2, unlike the simulated values. Is there something that may have caused this in the way that summary.fitted.values are computed?

Thank you,
Mark Myer
myer...@gmail.com
ORISE Fellow, US EPA ORD

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] summary.fitted.values and simulated responses differ
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] summary.fitted.values and simulated responses differ
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

"fitted.values" in INLA refers to the link-transformed predictor, and
_not_ to response level distributions.
You should compare the mean from fitted values to the mean of mu.i
from your other simulations.

For response level distributions in INLA, the common method is to use
inla.posterior.sample combined with response level sampling (or direct
weighting of probability functions/densities to reduce the Monte Carlo
variance; this can also be done in one call with inlabru::predict()
but I'm not sure if your models are supported by inlabru at this
time).

Finn

messages.subject: Grouping Time Structure
messages.subject_clean: Grouping Time Structure
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I am constructing a model for an hourly time series data using AR(1) processes for every day throughout the course of the year. I would like to group my data by day and then see how the rho parameters for each day are correlated. Am I correct in using the following to do this?

formula <- y ~ f(time.hour, model = "ar1",
                 group = time.day, control.group = list(model = "ar1"))

mod <- inla(formula, data = data, family = "gaussian")

Can I then interpret the groupRho parameters as the parameter for how my rho for each day changes over time?

Thanks,
Eric

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Grouping Time Structure
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Grouping Time Structure
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
The group rho in that model should tell you how similar the daily hourly cycle is from day to day; a value close to 1 would mean that the cycle changes slowly over the year.
The hourly process rho will model how variable the cycle is within the day.

The group rho does not however say how the rho for the hourly process changes over time, since both rho parameters are global; they are fixed over time. Only the process itself changes from day to day, not its dependence parameters.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Grouping Time Structure
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Grouping Time Structure
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Varying rho across the year (with a process model for rho itself) doesn’t fall under the latent Gaussian framework that inla handles; only a single layer of latent Gaussian can be present. The parameters of those Gaussians need in practice have low (ca 5-15) total dimension, and 365 is quite a lot in that context.  However, if you restrict rho to vary only slowly over the year (e.g. with logit(rho) the weighted sum of a few harmonic functions), there may be a way to achieve what you’re looking for,
by using the inla rgeneric framework, that allows you to define arbitrary precision models in R code. With that, you can define a joint model for all your daily time series, with a few parameters defining the block-diagonal precision matrix  Look for examples of rgeneric on the r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> site.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatially varying logistic regression with large data - INLA is crashing
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatially varying logistic regression with large data - INLA is crashing
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I managed to make it work. The reason why such a large model worked on my virtual machine but not on the server was rather simple but took me a few weeks to figure out: On the virtual machine, the table is automatically reordered using "amdc". on the server, INLA did not choose to use "amdc" on its own and thus crashed for anything above 200,000. Simply adding control.inla(....., reordering = "amdc") solved the problem and all models I wanted to evaluate ran like a charm on the server and finished in 1-2 days. May this info be of use for someone else with a similar problem someday...

If someone wants to add a few sentences what "amdc" actually does, feel free to enlighten me.

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

The model below fit a seasonal effect. doy stands for day of year and ranges from 255 to 333. spde_doy is a pcmatern SPDE based on a 1D mesh.

model <- bru(
  Count ~ season(map = doy, model = spde_doy)
  family = "nbinomial",
  data = final
)

I'd like to fit a model with a different seasonal pattern for each year. Every year has the same hyper parameters. The variable "iYear" in the data is an index of the year. It starts at 1 for the oldest year.

My attempts are

model <- bru(
  Count ~ season(map = doy, model = spde_doy, group = iYear) ,
  family = "nbinomial",
  data = final
)
Error in INLA::f(xxx, ..., group = group, model = model) : object 'iYear' not found

model <- bru(
  Count ~ season(map = doy, model = spde_doy, group = "iYear") ,
  family = "nbinomial",
  data = final
)
Error in (function (data, model, stackmaker, n = 10, result = NULL, family, : INLA returned message: object 'season.group' not found

model <- bru(
  Count ~ season(map = doy, model = spde_doy, group = final$iYear) ,
  family = "nbinomial",
  data = final
)
Error in (function (data, model, stackmaker, n = 10, result = NULL, family, : INLA returned message: object 'season.group' not found

model <- bru(
  Count ~ season(map = doy, model = spde_doy, replicate = final$iYear) ,
  family = "nbinomial",
  data = final
)
Error in (function (data, model, stackmaker, n = 10, result = NULL, family, : INLA returned message: length(replicate) != length(xx) 1796 != 1825

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Too flexible SPDE in a spatial poisson model?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Too flexible SPDE in a spatial poisson model?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Sorry for barging in in someone else's thread but:

if I understood correctly, when running a Poisson model with spde, the range and sd should be "thought of" in the log scale? So, when I set the pc.priors for the spde, if I want the prior for the range to be  P(range<200) = 0.01 I should set it: prior.range = c(log(200), 0.01)

Is that correct?

Thanks for the clarification!

El dijous, 18 agost de 2016 14:02:37 UTC+2, Geir-Arne Fuglstad va escriure:

> On Thu, 18 Aug 2016 at 11:16 Gustaf Rydevik <gustaf....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > The dataset is measured in meters and covers Scotland, so the range is about 300 000 x 300 000. Given that, I assume that an Rho0 of 100k would be a sensible starting point? I think I still don't have a very clear intuitive understanding of what Rho actually means...
>
> I think that makes sense. In the function you use to construct the SPDE object, the parameter rho is the distance at which the correlation between the values of the spatial effect at two spatial locations is approximately 0.1.
>
> > Unfortunately, changing Rhos and Sigmas doesn't effect the actual results of the model, but identifying and removing the obvious misunderstandings are at least a step in the right direction (I'm getting a range of SPDE effects of +/- 5 on the log scale, fixed effects that are about 1, and an overall result that is quite clearly overfitting)
>
> If the spatial range is exp(5) = 148, that is very low for your domain size. If you set rho0 = 100000, you should see something very different than that.
>
> --
> Geir-Arne Fuglstad

messages.subject: INLA survival model under-utilizes my hardware, how do I speed it up?
messages.subject_clean: INLA survival model under-utilizes my hardware, how do I speed it up?
messages.body_plain:
I am estimating a recurrent event survival model with INLA. I have several million observations, from which I am taking a sample. The size of the sample is going to be a function of the model estimation speed. I used the kidney dataset to get the syntax of the model (see below). After playing with the kidney example, I started using my own data. To improve the performance I spun up a Linux2 server on AWS with 16 cores and added these three options:

num.threads = 15, blas.num.threads = 15, control.compute = list(openmp.strategy = "huge")

Originally, I only added the control.compute argument, but didn't see a huge change in performance. It looked like it was only using a single core. I tried adding the thread arguments, but it is basically running on a single core in the server environment.

Is there some option I am missing to speed this up?

Kidney example:

formula = inla.surv(time,status) ~ age + sex
        + f(id,model="iid", hyper = list(prec = list(param=c(1, 1))))

kid.inla = inla(formula, family="coxph", data=kidney,
                control.hazard = list(scale.model = TRUE),
                num.threads = 7)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Too flexible SPDE in a spatial poisson model?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Too flexible SPDE in a spatial poisson model?
messages.body_plain:
There are two different log-scales here:
1) loglinear predictor
2) internal log representation of the parameters.

For 1), yes, you need to think of the prior for sigma in terms of its effect on the logscsle of the loglinear predictor. But thats unrelated to issue 2). With pcmatern, the parameters are specified in the range&sigma scaled, regardless of how it may be represented internally.

For pcmatern, as should already be clear from ?inla.spde.pcmatern,
for range 200, use 200, not log(200)
for sigma, consider the sensible variability on the log of the Poisson expectation.

One possibility is to consider the standard deviation on the expectation scale, pick the desired quantile from that, and convert that to the sigma parameter in a lognormal distribution to use in the pcmatern definition. (But this is not necessarily more intuitive than considering sigma directly...)

Finn

messages.subject: Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed(), status 253
messages.subject_clean: Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed(), status 253
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I have a very large data set of 181362 rows and I am running R-inla with a list of fixed effects, as shown below

formula  <- presence ~ depth + slope + aspect + dist2coast + gannet_dist + day_of_season + SOURCE_DB + sediment + offset(logopp)

M1 <- inla(presence ~ 1,
           family            = "binomial",
           data              = dat,
           control.compute   = list(dic=TRUE, waic=TRUE),
           control.predictor = list(
             compute = TRUE,
             quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)
           ), verbose=TRUE, num.threads=1, control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb")
           )

All my covariates are standadized to avoid numeric problems. The output gives error message as:  Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed(), ... status 253

If I run under the simplest formula: presence ~ 1, it worked.

1) I have tried both options: num.threads=1 and control.inla = list(strategy = "gaussian", int.strategy = "eb") . However, it still gives the same error message.

2) Since my data contains 27 years of data, I tried to reduce the size of my data to reduce memory usage. However, the error message disappears only if I keep the last 4 years data (=37381 rows). This is not acceptable for me.

3) The full expected model that I would like to apply will contain also a year smoother as rw1 model and a spatial spde model. When I run the full model, it seems that it's working without a fast pompt of the error message. But I dont know how long will it last and whether it will show the same error message later, that's why I tried the simplier model above and encountered the error message.

My questions are:

1. is it possible that the full model can run without error while the simplier model gives crash error message? if so, then I can directly run my full model, just need to wait for a long time

2. any solutions to solve the crash, without compromising the size of my data or model complexity

3. if R-inla can not technically help. Is there any practical suggestions? for instance, reduce the model complexity...

Thanks very much

Chun Chen

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chun,

have you tried to take a sample of the data? This would help to determine whether it is just the data size (and your hardware - lack of memory?) or if the problem lies somewhere else. My suggestion is to run the model with e.g. a 10% subset of the data; you could group your sample by year:

 sample <- stratified(data, group = year, size = 0.1, keep.rownames = TRUE)

Did you check for data incosistencies including NA values? Also, you could run in verbose = TRUE to check where exactly the model crashes. Similarly, you might run the taskmanager to check if it crashes just because the memory is full.

I ran into a comparable issue with a large dataset and setting control.inla(......, reordering = "amdc") solved the issue.
